findings.summary: The three Costs sections are placed at the end of page 1 instead of the head of page 2, so the page's section numbering restarts mid-page and page 2 opens on an unheaded continuation.
findings.evidence: Page 1 heading order: "4. Generic Predicates" → "5. Brands & Results" → "6. Lookup Beats switch" → "1. Runtime Cost" → "2. Compile Cost" → "3. satisfies"; page 2 ("Costs & Cheat Sheet") then opens with a bare bullets block, "`satisfies` checks against the target and keeps literals.", before "4. Pick By Input".
findings.fix: Move the four blocks from "1. Runtime Cost" through the `satisfies` code example to the top of page 2, ahead of the three `satisfies` bullets, so page 1 ends at section 6 and page 2 runs 1→6 under its own title.

findings.summary: The `satisfies` vs `as` code comments are mutually inconsistent — no single `Config` makes both true, and `as Config` does not widen a property to `string`.
findings.evidence: "const cfg = { mode:'dark' } satisfies Config;" / "// cfg.mode stays 'dark' — tag survives" and "const bad = { mode:'dark' } as Config;" / "// bad.mode widens to string — tag lost"
findings.fix: Pin `Config` to a literal union (e.g. `type Config = { mode: 'dark' | 'light' }`) and change the second comment to `// bad.mode becomes 'dark' | 'light' — the specific tag is lost`. (If `Config` declared `mode: string`, `satisfies` would widen too: the contextual type drives widening, as in the TS 4.9 `palette.green: string` example.)

findings.summary: "Nest the unions" is not a valid remedy for checker slowdown because TypeScript eagerly flattens nested unions, and module splitting does not change relation-checking cost either.
findings.evidence: "Unions with hundreds of members slow the checker down." … "Nest the unions or split them across modules."
findings.fix: Replace with remedies that actually reduce checker work: prefer a base type/interface hierarchy over a huge union, keep discriminated unions shallow with a single narrow discriminant, and annotate rather than re-infer at each narrowing site (see microsoft/TypeScript#42075 on eager union flattening and the TypeScript Performance wiki).

findings.summary: The "5. Brands & Results" section asserts the Result pattern but shows an example only for brands, so the Result type is never shown.
findings.evidence: Code block shows only `type UserId = string & { __brand: 'UserId' }` and `isUserId`, while the bullets claim "Result narrowing replaces try/catch." and "Error handling becomes exhaustive, not optional."
findings.fix: Add the Result type to the code block — `type Result<T,E> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: E }` with a one-line `if (r.ok)` narrowing — so the two Result bullets have a referent.

findings.summary: Two validation-cost bullets are appended to the mapped-type lookup section with an adversative "But", making payload-validation cost read as a drawback of the lookup table.
findings.evidence: "The mapped type forces every case — no `assertNever` needed." is followed by "But a full schema check per response costs real CPU." and "Validate once at the boundary, then trust the type inward."
findings.fix: Move those two bullets into the Runtime Cost section, which already carries the "deep validator | O(payload)" row, and close section 6 with an actual trade-off of the lookup form (it requires a total map, and unlike a switch it has no fallthrough branch).

findings.summary: The page title advertises breakage material that appears nowhere on the page.
findings.evidence: page_title is "Breakage & Advanced Patterns", but every block on the page is an advanced pattern or a cost section — no block covers callback invalidation, `let` vs `const` narrowing loss, aliasing, or widened discriminants.
findings.fix: Either retitle the page "Advanced Patterns" to match its contents, or add the breakage section here — minimally the callback trap (`if (x) { arr.forEach(() => x.foo()) }` versus the `const v = x` fix), which page 2's cheat sheet already assumes the reader has seen ("Narrowing lost inside callbacks.", "Copy narrowed values into `const` locals before closures or calls.").

findings.summary: Bullets attached to "6. Lookup Beats switch" attribute a per-response runtime CPU cost to a construct that is erased at compile time.
findings.evidence: Under the mapped-type code `type H = { [K in Shape['kind']]: (s: Extract<Shape,{kind:K}>) => number }`: "The mapped type forces every case — no `assertNever` needed." followed by "But a full schema check per response costs real CPU."
findings.fix: Move the last two bullets ("But a full schema check per response costs real CPU." / "Validate once at the boundary, then trust the type inward.") under "1. Runtime Cost", where the `deep validator — O(payload)` row sits; the mapped type has zero runtime cost, so the "But" contrast is false where it stands.

findings.summary: "`as` widens them and silences checking" misstates assertion semantics: `as` re-types to the target (often narrowing), and assertions between insufficiently overlapping types are still rejected.
findings.fix: Reword to "`as` replaces the inferred type with the declared one and suppresses the assignability check (only wholly unrelated types still error)."
